name: Tyler Hoffman
headline: 23, overnight home-care aide, Columbus, Ohio
title: Saturday Kickoff
situation: On a September Saturday, Tyler's dad calls to say the neighbors are gathering at the house for the Ohio State game. He mentions that John is bringing chili and the Millers are bringing meatballs, then adds, 'Grab a twelve-pack or a bag of chips if you want.' Tyler had planned to spend the afternoon reviewing the phlebotomy course schedule online and running errands. He knows these watch parties have unwritten rules around kickoff: show up before the game starts, make small talk during commercials, bring something to contribute, and don't slip out early. Empty-handed guests are noticed in his parents' neighborhood, and so is obvious disinterest in the game.

context.relationship_profiles:
His dad leaves decisions open-ended, so Tyler carries the guilt of skipping himself.
His mom files away absences and may mention them offhand later.
John and the Millers have known Tyler since childhood and always ask what he's 'doing now,' which he finds gently uncomfortable.
context.tendencies:
When a new program starts, Tyler treats it as urgent and reschedules social plans around it for the first month.
At past watch parties he arrived near kickoff and never missed one entirely, though he drifted to the porch by the second quarter.
He has texted his family to back out of plans before, citing homework or errands, and they accepted it without pushback.
context.current_state:
He's a few weeks into the phlebotomy program, unsure whether weekend classes will stick while he works third shift.
He's running short on sleep from the week's overnights.
His errands include picking up the course textbook.
context.immediate_memories:
The offer of a twelve-pack or chips pulls up last year's party, when he arrived with pretzels and his mom handed him the chip bowl so he'd look prepared.
'Kickoff' recalls his dad's rule that no one answers their phone during the first half.
context.reflective_memories:
He remembers his dad driving him to community college without mentioning cost — just dropping him off, his family's way of showing support.
He also felt easiest at a small Sunday dinner with only his parents, no neighbors asking what he was doing next.
